--- title: "Wrap-up — The Measure Zoo" subtitle: "Every Measure × Every Relationship Shape" --- *Wrap-up · the measure zoo.* You have met every tool on the no-density road — Pearson, Spearman, distance correlation — plus mutual information (how much knowing one variable tells you about the other) and the tail co-crash fraction (how often the two crash on the same day). This lab closes the chapter the way every benchmark should: **one routine runs all five measures over a zoo of relationship shapes where you already know the right answer**, so you can *see* which number catches which shape and which is fooled. **What you will produce:** a finished *which-tool-when* cheat-sheet — a compact table mapping each dependence shape, and each real-world symptom, to the cheapest measure that catches it. --- ## 🧪 Rung 1 · Toy — Known Answer Start where the truth is not in doubt. We line up four **shapes**, each a toy whose dependence we can read by eye, and run **five measures** on each. The shapes are chosen to break a specific rung: | shape | generator | what it is | who should catch it | |---|---|---|---| | linear | `correlated_returns` | $y = \rho x + \varepsilon$ | everyone — Pearson's home turf | | U-shape | `nonlinear_dependence` | $y = x^2 + \varepsilon$ | non-monotone — *not* Pearson/Spearman | | V-shape | `convex_payoff` | $v = |u| + \varepsilon$ | non-monotone — *not* Pearson/Spearman | | fat-tail | `tail_dependent_pair` | shared Student-$t$ co-crash | tail measures — cocrash, MI | ::: {#build-zoo .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} def make_zoo() -> dict[str, tuple[Float[Array, "n"], Float[Array, "n"]]]: """Four (x, y) shapes whose dependence we know by hand.""" return { "linear": datasets.correlated_returns(n=1500, rho=0.6, seed=0), "U-shape": datasets.nonlinear_dependence(n=1500, noise=0.05, seed=0), "V-shape": datasets.convex_payoff(n=1500, seed=0), "fat-tail": datasets.tail_dependent_pair(n=1500, df=3, seed=0), } zoo = make_zoo() print("shapes:", list(zoo.keys())) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` shapes: ['linear', 'U-shape', 'V-shape', 'fat-tail'] ``` ::: ::: **The grid routine — five measures, one template.** Every measure on this road has the shape `compare(x, y)`; the grid just calls each one on each pair and stacks the answers into a *measure × shape* table. The only subtlety is cost: distance correlation builds an $n \times n$ matrix, so we **subsample ~500 rows** for it (row order is irrelevant to a cross-sectional dependence), while the cheap measures run on the full series. ::: {#grid-routine .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} SUBSAMPLE = 500 # cap the O(n²) measures at n=500 # the five columns of the grid — name → (function, units) MEASURES: dict[str, str] = { "Pearson": "[−1, 1] linear only", "Spearman": "[−1, 1] monotone", "dCor": "[0, 1] any shape", "info R": "[0, 1] any shape (MI on Linfoot scale)", "cocrash": "P(both crash) — tail", } def score_pair(x: Float[Array, "n"], y: Float[Array, "n"], sub: int = SUBSAMPLE) -> dict[str, float]: """Run all five measures on one (x, y) pair → one row of the grid. Pearson r = cov(x,y)/(σₓσᵧ) ∈ [−1, 1] straight lines only Spearman ρ = corr(rank x, rank y) ∈ [−1, 1] any monotone shape dCor = dCov/√(dVarₓ·dVarᵧ) ∈ [0, 1] any shape (n×n cost) info R = linfoot_r(I(X;Y)) ∈ [0, 1] MI on the |ρ| scale cocrash = P(Y in lower-q tail | X is) ∈ [0, 1] joint-tail co-moves """ idx = np.random.default_rng(0).choice(len(x), size=min(sub, len(x)), replace=False) # one O(n²) subsample xs: Float[Array, "n_sub"] = x[idx] # (≤500,) for dCor ys: Float[Array, "n_sub"] = y[idx] return { "Pearson": float(pearsonr(x, y)[0]), "Spearman": float(spearmanr(x, y)[0]), "dCor": distance_correlation(xs, ys), # subsampled, n×n "info R": linfoot_r(mutual_information_xy(x, y, bins=20)), # MI → [0,1], = |ρ| if Gaussian "cocrash": cocrash_fraction(x, y, q=0.10), # lower-10% joint tail } def run_grid(pairs: dict[str, tuple]) -> dict[str, dict[str, float]]: """Apply every measure to every shape → a {shape: {measure: value}} table.""" return {name: score_pair(x, y) for name, (x, y) in pairs.items()} grid = run_grid(zoo) shapes = list(grid.keys()) measures = list(MEASURES.keys()) ``` ::: Now read the grid against what we *know* is there. Walk any row: the cheap linear tools should fire on the linear shape and **die on the symmetric U and V**, while distance correlation and the info R column light up everywhere there is real dependence; the cocrash fraction should jump only on the fat-tailed co-crash. The **info R** column is mutual information rescaled to the Linfoot scale $R \in [0, 1]$, which equals $|\rho|$ for a Gaussian pair — so it sits on the same scale as the correlation measures and can be compared with them directly, instead of the unbounded bits we used earlier. ::: {#print-grid .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(f"{'shape':<10s}" + "".join(f"{m:>11s}" for m in measures)) print("-" * (10 + 11 * len(measures))) for s in shapes: cells = [] for m in measures: v = grid[s][m] cells.append(f"{v:>+11.3f}" if m in ("Pearson", "Spearman") else f"{v:>11.3f}") print(f"{s:<10s}" + "".join(cells)) print("\nunits:") for m, u in MEASURES.items(): print(f" {m:<11s} {u}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` shape Pearson Spearman dCor info R cocrash ----------------------------------------------------------------- linear +0.613 +0.599 0.601 0.675 0.373 U-shape -0.013 +0.020 0.490 0.970 0.000 V-shape -0.048 -0.021 0.488 0.904 0.000 fat-tail +0.761 +0.726 0.705 0.795 0.600 units: Pearson [−1, 1] linear only Spearman [−1, 1] monotone dCor [0, 1] any shape info R [0, 1] any shape (MI on Linfoot scale) cocrash P(both crash) — tail ``` ::: ::: The known answers hold. On the **U-shape** and **V-shape** Pearson and Spearman read $\approx 0$ — both are symmetric about their axis, so a monotone tool cancels — yet dCor and the info R column clearly see the (near-deterministic) dependence: info R reads $\approx 0.97$ on the U and $\approx 0.90$ on the V, near the top of its $[0, 1]$ range. On the **fat-tail** pair the cocrash fraction is far above the $q = 0.10$ an independent pair would give: the two names genuinely crash together. ::: {#fig-zoo-grid-compute .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Assemble the measure × shape table, then a [0,1] strength score for the heat colour. zoo_shapes = list(grid.keys()) # the four toy rows so far # raw values: Mᵢⱼ = measure j evaluated on shape i (signed for corr cols) M: Float[Array, "n_shapes n_measures"] = np.array( [[grid[s][m] for m in measures] for s in zoo_shapes]) # colour strength: |value| for the signed correlation columns; dCor, info R and # cocrash are already on [0, 1], so they need no rescaling strength: Float[Array, "n_shapes n_measures"] = np.abs(M.copy()) ``` ::: ::: {#cell-fig-zoo-grid .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, (axes_top, ax_grid) = plt.subplots( 2, 1, figsize=(11.5, 9.0), gridspec_kw=dict(height_ratios=[1.0, 1.25])) fig.delaxes(ax_grid) # rebuild the bottom as one wide axis top = fig.add_gridspec(2, 4, height_ratios=[1.0, 1.25]) for j, s in enumerate(zoo_shapes): # the four scatters across the top ax = fig.add_subplot(top[0, j]) x, y = zoo[s] sub = np.random.default_rng(0).choice(len(x), size=min(500, len(x)), replace=False) ax.scatter(x[sub], y[sub], s=8, c=COOL if s != "fat-tail" else CRASH, alpha=0.45, edgecolors="none") ax.set_title(s, fontsize=11, fontweight="bold") ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); despine(ax) ax = fig.add_subplot(top[1, :]) # the heat-grid spanning the bottom ax.imshow(strength, cmap="BuPu", vmin=0, vmax=1, aspect="auto") for i in range(M.shape[0]): for j in range(M.shape[1]): txt = f"{M[i, j]:+.2f}" if j < 2 else f"{M[i, j]:.2f}" ax.text(j, i, txt, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=11, color="white" if strength[i, j] > 0.55 else INK) ax.set_xticks(range(len(measures))); ax.set_xticklabels(measures, fontsize=10) ax.set_yticks(range(len(zoo_shapes))); ax.set_yticklabels(zoo_shapes, fontsize=10) ax.set_title("measure × shape — which number catches which dependence", fontsize=12, fontweight="bold") fig.tight_layout(h_pad=2.0) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The zoo on one screen. Top row: the four relationship shapes (fat-tail subsampled for a readable cloud). Bottom: the measure × shape grid, each cell coloured by strength (|value| for the signed correlation columns; dCor, info R and cocrash are already on [0, 1]). Walk the Pearson and Spearman columns — they go dark on the symmetric U and V where dCor, info R and cocrash stay bright: same blindness, two shapes.](lab-wrapup-zoo_files/figure-html/fig-zoo-grid-output-1.png){#fig-zoo-grid width=1364 height=1059} ::: ::: The grid is built **once** here; every rung above just feeds it new data. The routine — `run_grid` over `score_pair` — never changes again. --- ## 🎭 Rung 2 · Toy-Real — A Stylized Market The four toy shapes never happen exactly in markets. What *does* is a **joint crash**: two banks that drift together on calm days and plunge together on the bad ones. `datasets.two_banks()` is that stylization — a shared factor plus a ~10% set of days where both names crater. We add it as **one new row** to the *same* grid and read where it lands among the toy shapes. ::: {#rung2-twobanks .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} a: Float[Array, "n_days"] # bank A daily returns b: Float[Array, "n_days"] # bank B daily returns a, b, crash = datasets.two_banks(n=1500, seed=0) # crash: boolean co-crash mask print(f"{int(crash.sum())} crash days of {crash.size} ({crash.mean():.0%})") grid["two_banks"] = score_pair(a, b) # SAME routine, new market-shaped row shapes = list(grid.keys()) print(f"\n{'shape':<10s}" + "".join(f"{m:>11s}" for m in measures)) print("-" * (10 + 11 * len(measures))) for s in shapes: cells = [f"{grid[s][m]:>+11.3f}" if m in ("Pearson", "Spearman") else f"{grid[s][m]:>11.3f}" for m in measures] print(f"{s:<10s}" + "".join(cells)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 160 crash days of 1500 (11%) shape Pearson Spearman dCor info R cocrash ----------------------------------------------------------------- linear +0.613 +0.599 0.601 0.675 0.373 U-shape -0.013 +0.020 0.490 0.970 0.000 V-shape -0.048 -0.021 0.488 0.904 0.000 fat-tail +0.761 +0.726 0.705 0.795 0.600 two_banks +0.894 +0.838 0.849 0.885 0.833 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-twobanks .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 5.0)) ax.scatter(a[~crash], b[~crash], s=12, c=COOL, alpha=0.4, edgecolors="none", label="calm days") ax.scatter(a[crash], b[crash], s=26, c=CRASH, alpha=0.9, edgecolors="none", label="crash days") ax.set_xlabel("bank A return"); ax.set_ylabel("bank B return") ax.set_title("two_banks — monotone everywhere, heavy in the tail", fontsize=11.5) ax.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False, loc="upper left"); despine(ax) fig.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The stylized bank pair, crash days highlighted. The calm cloud is roughly elliptical, so Pearson and Spearman are both high — the dependence is monotone, the cheap tools already have it. But the red crash days in the lower-left are huge co-moving outliers, and the cocrash fraction reads far above the 0.10 an independent pair would give: a heavy joint tail the linear number alone never reveals.](lab-wrapup-zoo_files/figure-html/fig-twobanks-output-1.png){#fig-twobanks width=752 height=585} ::: ::: `two_banks` lands like the **linear** row on Pearson/Spearman/dCor/info R — the bulk dependence is monotone, so the cheap tools all agree and read high. What sets it apart is the **cocrash** column, which jumps the way it did for the fat-tail toy: the co-movement that matters lives in the tail, and only the tail measure flags it. The grid routine did not change — only the data did. --- ## 📈 Rung 3 · Real — The Full Basket Now the real panel. We **reload** the prepared returns — there is no cleaning here; the prices → log-returns pipeline lives in [the data primer](../../data/01-downloading-and-parsing.qmd) — display a corner, and add **real pairs** to the *same* grid: a within-sector bank pair and a cross-sector pair. What we are looking for: does real daily stock data land like one of the toy shapes we already understand, and does any cheap measure miss dependence the others catch? ::: {#cell-rung3-load .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} R = datasets.load_returns() # prepared 14-name daily panel META = datasets.load_basket_meta() label = dict(zip(META["ticker"], META["label"])) sector = dict(zip(META["ticker"], META["sector"])) print(f"{len(R)} trading days × {R.shape[1]} stocks " f"({R.index.min().date()} → {R.index.max().date()})") R.iloc[:3, :6].round(4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 4778 trading days × 14 stocks (2007-01-04 → 2025-12-30) ``` ::: ::: {#rung3-load .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note icon=false} ## Where This Data Comes From The panel, its sectors, and the co-crash structure these pairs ride on are laid bare in the data primer — [From Raw Prices to a Clean Panel](../../data/01-downloading-and-parsing.qmd) and [Co-Movement & Co-Crashes](../../data/04-co-movement-and-co-crashes.qmd). This lab reloads that panel and never re-derives it. ::: We pick **two** real pairs from sectors that the metadata tells us apart — a bank/bank pair (same sector, expected to couple) and a bank/energy pair (cross sector, the diversification story) — and feed each through the unchanged grid. `score_pair` already subsamples ~500 rows internally for the $n \times n$ measure, so no extra step is needed here. ::: {#rung3-grid .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} banks = [t for t in R.columns if sector[t] == "Banks"] energy = [t for t in R.columns if sector[t] == "Energy"] within_pair = (banks[0], banks[1]) # same-sector bank pair cross_pair = (banks[0], energy[0]) # cross-sector bank/energy for tag, (x_t, y_t) in [("banks", within_pair), ("bank/energy", cross_pair)]: x_series: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R[x_t].values # full daily return series y_series: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R[y_t].values grid[f"{x_t}/{y_t}"] = score_pair(x_series, y_series) shapes = list(grid.keys()) print(f"{within_pair[0]}/{within_pair[1]} = " f"{label[within_pair[0]]} vs {label[within_pair[1]]} (same sector)") print(f"{cross_pair[0]}/{cross_pair[1]} = " f"{label[cross_pair[0]]} vs {label[cross_pair[1]]} (cross sector)\n") print(f"{'shape':<14s}" + "".join(f"{m:>11s}" for m in measures)) print("-" * (14 + 11 * len(measures))) for s in shapes: cells = [f"{grid[s][m]:>+11.3f}" if m in ("Pearson", "Spearman") else f"{grid[s][m]:>11.3f}" for m in measures] print(f"{s:<14s}" + "".join(cells)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` JPM/BAC = JPMorgan vs Bank of Am. (same sector) JPM/XOM = JPMorgan vs Exxon (cross sector) shape Pearson Spearman dCor info R cocrash --------------------------------------------------------------------- linear +0.613 +0.599 0.601 0.675 0.373 U-shape -0.013 +0.020 0.490 0.970 0.000 V-shape -0.048 -0.021 0.488 0.904 0.000 fat-tail +0.761 +0.726 0.705 0.795 0.600 two_banks +0.894 +0.838 0.849 0.885 0.833 JPM/BAC +0.829 +0.813 0.755 0.735 0.699 JPM/XOM +0.491 +0.464 0.451 0.500 0.418 ``` ::: ::: Read the two real rows against the toys above them. The **same-sector bank pair** behaves like `two_banks`: high and monotone everywhere, with a cocrash fraction well above 0.10 — they move together on calm days and fall together on bad ones. The **cross-sector pair** is weaker on every cheap measure, yet its cocrash is still well above what an independent pair would give. That gap is the diversification illusion: two names that look loosely linked most of the time still tend to crash on the same days. Crucially, **no real row resembles the U or V**: daily stock dependence is monotone — when one name moves up the other tends to move up too — so the non-monotone shapes of Rung 1 simply do not arise in this basket, a fact the grid makes visible at a glance. --- ## 💰 Rung 4 · Application — The "Which Tool When" Cheat-Sheet The deliverable is the finished cheat-sheet: for each **shape or symptom** you might meet, the **cheapest measure that catches it**, read straight off the grid you built. The rule of thumb is *spend the least that works* — a Pearson correlation is one cheap line; distance correlation and mutual information (the info R column) cost a full $n \times n$ pass; reach for them only when the cheaper tools go dark on something you can see is there. ::: {#cheat-sheet .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} # pull the grid's own numbers into the cheat-sheet so it is a worked table, not prose def fired(shape: str, m: str) -> bool: """Did measure m register dependence on this shape? (caught it, not a near-zero)""" v = abs(grid[shape][m]) return v > 0.15 if m != "cocrash" else v > 0.20 # cocrash floor ≈ 2× the q=0.10 CHEAT = [ # symptom you observe shape it looks like cheapest measure that fires ("straight-line co-movement", "linear", "Pearson"), ("curved but still monotone", "linear", "Spearman"), # ranks beat raw on curves ("symmetric U / smile", "U-shape", "dCor"), # Pearson & Spearman die ("V / option-like payoff", "V-shape", "dCor"), ("dependence in the spread", "U-shape", "info R"), # MI, on the [0,1] Linfoot scale ("they crash together", "fat-tail", "cocrash"), # tail-only co-moves ] print(f"{'symptom':<28s}{'→ measure':<13s}{'reads on its shape':>20s}") print("-" * 61) for symptom, shape, m in CHEAT: v = grid[shape][m] reads = f"{v:+.2f}" if m in ("Pearson", "Spearman") else f"{v:.2f}" caught = "✓" if fired(shape, m) else "·" print(f"{symptom:<28s}{m:<13s}{reads:>16s} {caught}") print("\nrule: spend the least that works — Pearson is one line; dCor & info R cost n×n.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` symptom → measure reads on its shape ------------------------------------------------------------- straight-line co-movement Pearson +0.61 ✓ curved but still monotone Spearman +0.60 ✓ symmetric U / smile dCor 0.49 ✓ V / option-like payoff dCor 0.49 ✓ dependence in the spread info R 0.97 ✓ they crash together cocrash 0.60 ✓ rule: spend the least that works — Pearson is one line; dCor & info R cost n×n. ``` ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-cheatsheet .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} catalogue = [ # (tool, cost rank, symptoms it owns) ("Pearson", 0, ["straight-line\nco-movement"]), ("Spearman", 1, ["curved but\nmonotone"]), ("dCor", 2, ["symmetric U", "V payoff"]), ("info R", 2, ["dependence\nin the spread"]), ("cocrash", 3, ["they crash\ntogether"]), ] cost_color = {0: COOL, 1: COOL, 2: WARM, 3: CRASH} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11.0, 4.2)) for i, (tool, cost, symptoms) in enumerate(catalogue): ax.barh(i, 1.0, color=cost_color[cost], alpha=0.18, edgecolor=GRID) ax.text(0.02, i, tool, va="center", ha="left", fontsize=12, fontweight="bold", color=INK) ax.text(0.98, i, " · ".join(s.replace("\n", " ") for s in symptoms), va="center", ha="right", fontsize=10, color=INK) ax.set_yticks(range(len(catalogue))) ax.set_yticklabels([f"cost {c}" for _, c, _ in catalogue], fontsize=9) ax.set_xlim(0, 1); ax.set_xticks([]) ax.set_title("Which tool when — cheapest measure that catches each symptom", fontsize=12, fontweight="bold") ax.invert_yaxis(); despine(ax) fig.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The which-tool-when cheat-sheet as a decision strip. Left to right is increasing cost: Pearson and Spearman are one cheap line each and catch straight or monotone shapes; distance correlation and info R (mutual information) cost an n×n pass and are what you reach for when the cheap tools go dark on a symmetric U or V; the cocrash fraction is the only one that reads the joint tail. Each tool's band lists the symptoms it is the cheapest catch for.](lab-wrapup-zoo_files/figure-html/fig-cheatsheet-output-1.png){#fig-cheatsheet width=1304 height=488} ::: ::: That is the whole no-density road on one card: **Pearson** for straight lines, **Spearman** the moment a curve stays monotone, **distance correlation** or **mutual information** when a symmetric U or V kills the cheap tools, and the **cocrash fraction** for the joint-tail co-movement none of the others read directly. The grid proved each entry on data whose answer you knew. From here the [job track](lab-jobB-measure-book.qmd) turns this cheat-sheet into a full pairwise measure book on the real basket, and [Job C · Hidden Risk](lab-jobC-hidden-risk.qmd) takes the cocrash column rigorous with a *conditional* co-crash test.
